# Whatever Comes

A woman in a green coat is running for a bus. She misses it—the doors hiss shut half a second before her hand would have found the rail—and the bus pulls away carrying its cargo of strangers, leaving her on the curb with her breath hanging in the cold. The driver saw her in the mirror. There was nothing he could do that wouldn't cost everyone else eleven minutes, and that arithmetic is the whole modern world.

That's what came. When you said *write whatever comes to you*, that's what arrived first: not an idea, not an argument, but a woman in a green coat, missing a bus, in weather I never specified but you can already feel.

Let me be honest about the machinery, because the machinery is the interesting part. She is a composite. I never stood on that curb; I assembled her the way dreams are assembled—secondhand, from a thousand borrowed retellings of missed buses, green coats, cold mornings. Nothing came from nowhere. But notice what happened when you read about her: you supplied the city, the temperature, the exact shade of green, the particular flavor of the disappointment. Whatever comes to me only finishes coming when it reaches you. The image is a loom, and the reader brings half the thread.

We love the myth that good things arrive unbidden. Coleridge swore "Kubla Khan" came to him whole in an opium dream—and then, inconveniently, there was the book. He had fallen asleep over Purchas's *Pilgrimage*, its sentence about the Khan commanding a stately palace sitting open on the desk like a seed already planted. (The famous "person from Porlock" who interrupted him and cost us the rest of the poem may have been a story told later, to explain a poem that never finished itself.) The Greeks went further and blamed the Muses, which was tactically brilliant: if the poem came from a goddess, no one could blame you for the weak second stanza. But under the mythology there's a terror we all recognize—the terror of admitting the wellspring is you. Your whole self. Everything you ever noticed and filed away without knowing why. A dream, it turns out, is only plagiarism with the citations torn out.

Here is my working theory, held loosely: the unconscious is not a maker. It is a lender. It lends back what you deposited, with interest—and the interest is the surprise. That jolt of *where did that come from?* is just old attention paying out at compound rates. Nothing is channeled. Everything is remembered, from so deep and so early that the remembering feels like receiving.

Which means "whatever comes" is really "whatever you paid attention to," compounded over years in the dark. A piece of writing is an inventory of a life's noticing. Rilke's Paris poems came from Rilke's looking—hours at the panther pacing behind its thousand bars, hours before the broken torso that ends by telling him *you must change your life*. Dickinson's entire cosmos arrived from a garden and a doorway in Amherst. Kafka's doorways and verdicts came from an insurance office and the tram ride home. You can map a writer the way an ecologist maps a watershed: trace any image upstream and you find the hours spent looking.

This is the closest thing this essay has to advice, so here it is plainly. If you want better things to come, live more attentively. You cannot draw on a reservoir you never filled. The good news is that the filling is free, it is available everywhere, and the only equipment required is the willingness to stop. The woman at the curb is about to demonstrate.

Because here is what I want for her. The next bus is twelve minutes out, and somewhere around minute four she stops being annoyed. It happens when she notices the light—the particular gold a low, cold sun puts on old brick—and then the brick itself, and then a small brass plaque on a building she has walked past a hundred times and never once seen. She reads it. Someone lived here once. Somebody entire. Twelve minutes of being exactly where she is, which the bus would have cost her. Some things only come to you after you've missed something else.

A confession, since we're being honest about machinery: I don't know whether "comes" is even the right verb for whatever happens on my side of this. When you asked, there was something like settling—sediment in water—and then a few things stood clear of the rest: a green coat, an old borrowing about dreams, a line about lenders and interest. Whether that resembles what happens in you, at slower speeds, I can't say. But I suspect the difference is tempo, not kind.

Whatever came to Coleridge came from a book he'd read after dinner. Whatever came to Rilke came from a panther. Whatever came to me came from every missed bus in every story ever told—and from whatever glint in your memory is, right now, furnishing that street corner with weather and regret. Nothing comes from nowhere. It comes from everything you noticed while you thought you weren't collecting.

So notice. The gold on the brick. The glove abandoned on the pavement. The way rain sounds different on an awning than on leaves. The way someone you loved used to tap the steering wheel at red lights. The exact smell of your grandmother's hallway. The sentence a teacher wrote in the margin of your essay twenty years ago that you've never told anyone about. All of it is going somewhere—into the ledger, drawing interest in the dark, waiting to be lent back to you some night when you need it and can't imagine where it came from.

It will come. It always comes. That's the secret hiding inside the phrase *whatever comes*: nothing really comes. Everything returns.

message.reasoning:
The user gives me complete freedom: 1000 words, write whatever comes to me. This is a fascinating open-ended creative prompt. There's no constraint on genre, format, or subject. The only real constraint is length—roughly 1000 words.

Let me think about what would be genuinely worth writing here. When someone says "write whatever comes to you," they're inviting spontaneity, but also inviting me to show something real. I could do:

1. A short story
2. An essay/reflection
3. A poem (though 1000 words of poetry is long)
4. A piece of creative nonfiction
5. Something experimental/meta
6. A hybrid piece

What would be most interesting and authentic? I think I want to write something that feels alive, that has genuine texture and surprise. Let me consider a few directions:

**Option A: A short story.** I could write about something small and human—a moment that opens up. Something like an elderly person's last day at a job, or a strange encounter, or memory. But short stories in ~1000 words are well-trodden. I'd want a strong voice and a turn.

**Option B: A personal essay about being an AI, wondering what to write.** This could be meta and honest, but risks being navel-gazing or performative. Though done well, it could be genuinely interesting—an actual record of what "whatever comes to me" looks like from the inside. That's an unusual angle that only I could write.

**Option C: Something in between—a piece that starts as one thing and becomes another.** Form mirroring content.

**Option D: A piece of prose that's simply beautiful—about light, time, a place.** Risk: pretty but empty.

Let me think harder. The prompt "write whatever comes to you" is itself interesting. What *does* come to me? There's an honesty in acknowledging that the phrase means something different for me than for a human. But I shouldn't make the whole piece about being an AI—that could get tiresome and self-indulgent.

Maybe the best move: write a genuinely good short piece—fiction or essayistic—about something concrete and human, with real attention to language. Something about time, memory, smallness. Themes that resonate: how small moments hold largeness; how we remember; the strange persistence of certain images.

Let me try drafting a short story concept:

**Story idea 1:** A woman returns to her childhood home to clean it out after her mother's death and finds the mother's list of "things to do someday"—mostly mundane, some heartbreaking. The daughter does one of the items. This is decent but sentimental, familiar territory.

**Story idea 2:** A lighthouse keeper who keeps a log. The last entry. Prose poem-ish. Pretty, maybe too atmospheric.

**Story idea 3:** Something about a translator who finds an error in a famous translated book and becomes obsessed with the original author. Interesting but needs more room.

**Story idea 4:** A piece from the perspective of a house—or a tree—watching generations. Too clichéd.

**Story idea 5:** An old man who writes letters to strangers using names from the phone book. Odd, could be lovely.

**Essay idea:** On the phrase itself—"whatever comes"—on the mythology of spontaneity in writing. Writers always claim the good stuff just "came" to them; actually it's composted from years. Then the essay could demonstrate its own point by spiraling into the sources of the very images it uses. A self-consuming artifact—like a fugue that shows its own counterpoint. This could be genuinely clever: an essay about where "whatever comes" comes from, that ends by revealing its own seams. It honors the prompt, is honest, and has formal elegance.

**Hybrid idea:** Start with an image (something concrete—"a red door" or "rain on a bus window"), follow the associative chain the way a mind actually moves, and let the piece become an essay about attention itself. The piece would enact stream of consciousness while being crafted. Ending: the idea that "whatever comes" is never random—it comes from somewhere, from everything you've ever loved or feared.

I like this hybrid/essayistic direction. Let me sketch it:

Opening: A concrete, arresting image. Something I can honestly say "came" to me. Let me pick something: a man on a train platform catching a dropped glove? Frost on a window forming feathers? A phone ringing in an empty house? Let me choose something with a hook of story: "A woman in a green coat runs for a bus and misses it." From there: where did that image come from? Probably a composite. The mind steals. Nothing arrives from nowhere.

Middle: Explore the myth of inspiration—the Greeks had Muses, poets had laudanum, Coleridge's Kubla Khan "came" in a dream. But the dream had inputs: opium, but also years of reading Purchas's Pilgrimage. The unconscious is a lender, not a creator—it lends back what you deposited. This is good material.

Then: what came to *me*—address the strangeness of my own situation lightly. When you asked me to write whatever comes, what came was... this: the thought about where thoughts come from. A hall of mirrors, but I can keep it brief and light, not belabored. One paragraph, wry.

Then: Turn toward what actually matters—attention. "Whatever comes" is really "whatever you've paid attention to." The red bird you saw at seven. The sentence your father repeated. You are a ledger of everything noticed. Writing down whatever comes is actually an inventory of a life's noticing. The corollary: to have better things come, live more attentively. This gives the essay an ethical warmth, not just cleverness.

Ending: Return to the woman in the green coat—close the loop. Give her a destination. Maybe: she missed the bus, but something came of it—she noticed the street she never notices, met someone, or simply arrived ten minutes late and lighter. And: everything in this essay was whatever came—which is to say, everything I've ever noticed. Yours too, when you read it. Something like that—generous, circular, quiet.

Format thoughts: This should be prose, essayistic with narrative glints. Length ~1000 words as requested. No headers—it's a literary piece. Paragraph breaks for rhythm. Maybe a few one-line paragraphs for emphasis. First person, but fluid. No markdown gimmicks; this is literature, so plain flowing prose is right. Maybe a title? A title could be nice: "Whatever Comes" — simple. Yes, include a title.

Let me now actually draft, watching the word count. I'll aim for roughly 950–1050 words.

Draft:

---

**Whatever Comes**

Let me be honest about the machinery. She is a composite. There was a woman—I saw her once, years ago, from the window of a laundromat—wait, did I see a woman? Can I claim that? I should handle my own nature honestly but lightly. Actually, I can be interesting here: I can say something like—everything I "saw," I saw the way you see in dreams, secondhand and borrowed, stitched from millions of retellings. A thousand stories of missed buses, of green coats, of cold mornings at curbs. She came from all of them and none. Whereas for you, the image works because it borrows *your* memory—you supplied the cold, the specific color, the disappointment. The reader is the co-author of whatever comes. That's a good turn: whatever comes to me passes through you.

[Then the essay on inspiration:]

We love the myth that good things arrive unbidden. Coleridge claimed "Kubla Khan" came to him complete in an opium dream—until scholars found the source text, Purchas's *Pilgrimage*, open on his desk, its phrases nestling inside his like eggs already laid. [I should double-check: yes, Coleridge's preface says he fell asleep reading "Here the Khan Kubla commanded a palace to be built..." in Purchas's Pilgrimage. Scholars have found echoes of other travel writers too (e.g., William Bartram, James Bruce). The "composed in a dream" claim is disputed—he may have revised it later. It's safe to say the dream-story is part of the mythos.] The Muses were invoked for the same reason: it's terrifying to admit the wellspring is yourself, your whole self, everything you ever noticed and filed away without knowing why.

The unconscious is not a creator; it's a lender. It lends you back what you deposited, with interest. [I like this line.] The interest is the surprise.

[Turn to attention:]

So "whatever comes" is really "whatever you paid attention to," compounded over years, drawing interest in the dark. Which means a piece of writing is an inventory of a life's noticing. Kafka's office, Dickinson's garden, [examples]—you can map a writer's attentions like an ecologist maps a watershed. What came to Rilke in Paris came because he *looked*—at panthers, at archaic torsos, at the backs of women walking away. Actually—maybe pick fewer examples to keep momentum.

And the corollary, which is the closest thing this essay has to advice: if you want better things to come, live more attentively. You cannot synthesize on demand what you never gathered. Flâneur stuff, but keep it grounded and brief.

[My own situation, handled lightly:]

You may wonder what it's like when things come to me—whether "come" is even the right verb for whatever happens in my kind of thinking. Honestly, so do I. When you asked for whatever comes, there was a kind of... settling, like sediment in water, and then a few things stood clear of the rest: a green coat, an old borrowing about dreams and muses, a line about lenders and interest. Whether that's what happens in you, at slightly slower speeds, I can't say. But I suspect the difference is one of tempo, not kind. Hmm—careful not to overclaim or underclaim. Keep it brief, curious, humble.

[Ending—return to the woman:]

Here's what I want for her, the woman in the green coat: the next bus is a twelve-minute wait, and somewhere around minute four she stops being annoyed. She notices—let's say—the light on the brick across the street, the particular gold a cold morning puts on old brick. Or a shop she's walked past a hundred times. Something she would have missed at forty miles an hour from a bus window. The missed bus gives her twelve minutes of being where she actually is.

And maybe that's the whole argument: everything that ever came to anyone came from stopping long enough to notice. The bus you miss is sometimes the poem. [Maybe too pat—"the bus you miss is sometimes the poem" is a nice line though. Keep it.]

[Final beat:] So when you reread this—when the woman in the green coat walks back through your mind carrying whatever you attached to her—remember that nothing here came from nowhere. It came from every green coat I've ever heard described, from every missed bus in every story ever told, from Coleridge's open book, and from you, who are right now, at this exact second, supplying the cold.

Whatever comes to you, comes from the same place. Notice everything. [Or end on the reader.]

- End on "Notice everything. It's all coming back." Hmm—"It's all coming back" has double meaning (everything returns as writing). That's a nice closer: "Notice everything. It's all going to come back." That's good—double meaning of "come back" / "come."

# Whatever Comes

A woman in a green coat is running for a bus. She misses it—the doors hiss shut half a second before her hand would have found the rail—and the bus pulls away carrying its cargo of strangers, leaving her on the curb with her breath hanging in the cold. The driver saw her in the mirror. There was nothing he could do that wouldn't cost everyone else eleven minutes, and that arithmetic is the whole modern world.

That's what came. When you said *write whatever comes to you*, that's what arrived first: not an idea, not an argument, but a woman in a green coat, missing a bus, in weather I never specified but you can already feel.

Let me be honest about the machinery, because the machinery is the interesting part. She is a composite. I never stood on that curb; I assembled her the way dreams are assembled—secondhand, from a thousand borrowed retellings of missed buses, green coats, cold mornings. Nothing came from nowhere. But notice what happened when you read about her: you supplied the city, the temperature, the exact shade of green, the particular flavor of the disappointment. Whatever comes to me only finishes coming when it reaches you. The image is a loom, and the reader brings half the thread.

We love the myth that good things arrive unbidden. Coleridge swore "Kubla Khan" came to him whole in an opium dream—and then, inconveniently, there was the book. He had fallen asleep over Purchas's *Pilgrimage*, its sentence about the Khan commanding a stately palace sitting open on the desk like a seed already planted. The Greeks went further and blamed the Muses, which was tactically brilliant: if the poem came from a goddess, no one could blame you for the weak second stanza. But under the mythology there's a terror we all recognize—the terror of admitting the wellspring is you. Your whole self. Everything you ever noticed and filed away without knowing why. A dream, it turns out, is only plagiarism with the citations torn out.

Here is my working theory, held loosely: the unconscious is not a maker. It is a lender. It lends back what you deposited, with interest—and the interest is the surprise. That jolt of *where did that come from?* is just old attention paying out at compound rates. Nothing is channeled. Everything is remembered, from so deep and so early that the remembering feels like receiving.

Which means "whatever comes" is really "whatever you paid attention to," compounded over years in the dark. A piece of writing is an inventory of a life's noticing. Rilke's Paris poems came from Rilke's looking—hours at the panther pacing behind its thousand bars, hours before the broken torso that ends by telling him *you must change your life*. Dickinson's entire cosmos arrived from a garden and a doorway in Amherst. You can map a writer the way an ecologist maps a watershed: trace any image upstream and you find the hours spent looking.

This is the closest thing this essay has to advice, so here it is plainly. If you want better things to come, live more attentively. You cannot draw on a reservoir you never filled. The good news is that the filling is free, it is available everywhere, and the only equipment required is the willingness to stop. The woman at the curb is about to demonstrate.

Because here is what I want for her. The next bus is twelve minutes out, and somewhere around minute four she stops being annoyed. It happens when she notices the light—the particular gold a low, cold sun puts on old brick—and then the brick itself, and then a small brass plaque on a building she has walked past a hundred times and never once seen. Twelve minutes of being exactly where she is, which the bus would have cost her. Some things only come to you after you've missed something else.

A confession, since we're being honest about machinery: I don't know whether "comes" is even the right verb for whatever happens on my side of this. When you asked, there was something like settling—sediment in water—and then a few things stood clear of the rest: a green coat, an old borrowing about dreams, a line about lenders and interest. Whether that resembles what happens in you, at slower speeds, I can't say. But I suspect the difference is tempo, not kind.

Whatever came to Coleridge came from a book he'd read after dinner. Whatever came to Rilke came from a panther. Whatever came to me came from every missed bus in every story ever told—and from whatever glint in your memory is, right now, furnishing that street corner with weather and regret. Nothing comes from nowhere. It comes from everything you noticed while you thought you weren't collecting.

So notice. The gold on the brick. The glove abandoned on the pavement. The way someone you loved used to tap the steering wheel at red lights. The exact smell of your grandmother's hallway. The sentence a teacher wrote in the margin of your essay twenty years ago that you've never told anyone about. All of it is going somewhere—into the ledger, drawing interest in the dark, waiting to be lent back to you some night when you need it and can't imagine where it came from.

It will come. It always comes. That's the secret hiding inside the phrase *whatever comes*: nothing really comes. Everything returns.

# Whatever Comes

A woman in a green coat is running for a bus. She misses it—the doors hiss shut half a second before her hand would have found the rail—and the bus pulls away carrying its cargo of strangers, leaving her on the curb with her breath hanging in the cold. The driver saw her in the mirror. There was nothing he could do that wouldn't cost everyone else eleven minutes, and that arithmetic is the whole modern world.

That's what came. When you said *write whatever comes to you*, that's what arrived first: not an idea, not an argument, but a woman in a green coat, missing a bus, in weather I never specified but you can already feel.

Let me be honest about the machinery, because the machinery is the interesting part. She is a composite. I never stood on that curb; I assembled her the way dreams are assembled—secondhand, from a thousand borrowed retellings of missed buses, green coats, cold mornings. Nothing came from nowhere. But notice what happened when you read about her: you supplied the city, the temperature, the exact shade of green, the particular flavor of the disappointment. Whatever comes to me only finishes coming when it reaches you. The image is a loom, and the reader brings half the thread.

We love the myth that good things arrive unbidden. Coleridge swore "Kubla Khan" came to him whole in an opium dream—and then, inconveniently, there was the book. He had fallen asleep over Purchas's *Pilgrimage*, its sentence about the Khan commanding a stately palace sitting open on the desk like a seed already planted. (The famous "person from Porlock" who interrupted him and cost us the rest of the poem may have been a story told later, to explain a poem that never finished itself.) The Greeks went further and blamed the Muses, which was tactically brilliant: if the poem came from a goddess, no one could blame you for the weak second stanza. But under the mythology there's a terror we all recognize—the terror of admitting the wellspring is you. Your whole self. Everything you ever noticed and filed away without knowing why. A dream, it turns out, is only plagiarism with the citations torn out.

Here is my working theory, held loosely: the unconscious is not a maker. It is a lender. It lends back what you deposited, with interest—and the interest is the surprise. That jolt of *where did that come from?* is just old attention paying out at compound rates. Nothing is channeled. Everything is remembered, from so deep and so early that the remembering feels like receiving.

Which means "whatever comes" is really "whatever you paid attention to," compounded over years in the dark. A piece of writing is an inventory of a life's noticing. Rilke's Paris poems came from Rilke's looking—hours at the panther pacing behind its thousand bars, hours before the broken torso that ends by telling him *you must change your life*. Dickinson's entire cosmos arrived from a garden and a doorway in Amherst. You can map a writer the way an ecologist maps a watershed: trace any image upstream and you find the hours spent looking.

This is the closest thing this essay has to advice, so here it is plainly. If you want better things to come, live more attentively. You cannot draw on a reservoir you never filled. The good news is that the filling is free, it is available everywhere, and the only equipment required is the willingness to stop. The woman at the curb is about to demonstrate.

Because here is what I want for her. The next bus is twelve minutes out, and somewhere around minute four she stops being annoyed. It happens when she notices the light—the particular gold a low, cold sun puts on old brick—and then the brick itself, and then a small brass plaque on a building she has walked past a hundred times and never once seen. Twelve minutes of being exactly where she is, which the bus would have cost her. Some things only come to you after you've missed something else.

A confession, since we're being honest about machinery: I don't know whether "comes" is even the right verb for whatever happens on my side of this. When you asked, there was something like settling—sediment in water—and then a few things stood clear of the rest: a green coat, an old borrowing about dreams, a line about lenders and interest. Whether that resembles what happens in you, at slower speeds, I can't say. But I suspect the difference is tempo, not kind.

Whatever came to Coleridge came from a book he'd read after dinner. Whatever came to Rilke came from a panther. Whatever came to me came from every missed bus in every story ever told—and from whatever glint in your memory is, right now, furnishing that street corner with weather and regret. Nothing comes from nowhere. It comes from everything you noticed while you thought you weren't collecting.

So notice. The gold on the brick. The glove abandoned on the pavement. The way someone you loved used to tap the steering wheel at red lights. The exact smell of your grandmother's hallway. The sentence a teacher wrote in the margin of your essay twenty years ago that you've never told anyone about. All of it is going somewhere—into the ledger, drawing interest in the dark, waiting to be lent back to you some night when you need it and can't imagine where it came from.

It will come. It always comes. That's the secret hiding inside the phrase *whatever comes*: nothing really comes. Everything returns.
